one_liner: Discontinued C++ callback and callback-list (signal) headers; 2011 numbers beat Boost.Signals2 and tie libsigc++ on single calls.
what_it_does: GCallback<void (int)> is a type-erased callable (free function, member function plus object pointer, or functor), close to std::function in shape, built with makeCallback(&obj, &T::method). GCallbackList<void (int)> is a minimal signal: add() appends a callback, remove() and clear() blank entries, operator() calls every live callback in order. It returns nothing per slot, has no connection handles, combiners, blocking or slot tracking, so it is not a drop-in for Boost.Signals2 or libsigc++.
how_it_is_fast: GCallback stores the target in a small inline buffer and dispatches through a static per-type table of function pointers (a hand-rolled vtable: destroy, clone, invoker, isSame), so a call is two dependent loads and one indirect call with no locking. GCallbackList is a plain std::deque of GCallback walked by index, with no mutex, no copied slot-list snapshot, no combiner and no tracked-object locking; that missing machinery is where the 4x to 14x gap to the default thread-safe Boost.Signals2 signal comes from, and lower per-emission setup is why it leads libsigc++ at 5 to 10 slots.
when_to_use: Maintaining code that already uses cpgf (for example the author's gincu engine) and needs its callback lists.
Single-threaded event dispatch with a handful of listeners per event, where an unsynchronized vector-of-callbacks is all you need.
Reading a compact example of std::function-style type erasure with a function-pointer table instead of virtual functions.
New code only if you cannot take the author's successor, eventpp, which the README recommends for the callback list feature.
when_not_to_use: Any new project: the README says cpgf is not continued and points callback-list users to eventpp (already catalogued).
Multi-threaded emit or connect: GCallbackList has no locking and its const operator() erases cleared entries from a mutable deque during dispatch.
When you need connection objects, scoped disconnection, slot return values or combiners, or lifetime tracking (Boost.Signals2 and libsigc++ features absent here).
When the target is plain std::function speed: no benchmark against std::function exists, and the invoke path (base pointer, table pointer, indirect call) is not obviously cheaper.
Signals with dozens of slots: the lead over libsigc++ falls to 1.17x (VC 9) and 1.31x (GCC) at 50 slots, within the noise of this harness.

integration.form: header-only (include/cpgf/gcallback.h and gcallbacklist.h plus a few cpgf utility headers: gfunctiontraits.h, gtypetraits.h, gcompiler.h, gpp.h, gtypelist.h, gassert.h, genableif.h); the rest of cpgf is a CMake-built static library
integration.dependencies: none beyond the C++ standard library for the callback headers
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 since cpgf 1.6 (README: VC 2015 and GCC 4.9.1 tested, later GCC 7.3.0 and Clang 5.0.2 on Ubuntu 18.04); the library requires exceptions and RTTI, and an empty GCallback throws std::bad_function_call
integration.platforms: any (README lists Windows, Linux and macOS builds)
integration.thread_safety: none documented; GCallbackList has no mutex and mutates its deque inside the const call operator
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: no: different API from Boost.Signals2 and libsigc++ (no connections, combiners, slot tracking or return collection); GCallback alone is close to std::function but not a drop-in

gotchas: The published numbers measured the 2011 C++03 implementation (GCallbackList with GCallbackConnection over std::list, per the harness's commented typedef). Callback and callback list were rewritten in C++11 in March 2017 (commit history of gcallbacklist.h), while the harness (committed 2011-10-04, never updated) calls callbackList.add(&obj, &member) with two arguments, which the current one-argument add() does not accept; the harness also includes cpgf/testcase/benchmark/benchmarkcallback.h, a path that does not exist, and uses GWiseMap, which the callback headers no longer provide. The table therefore cannot be reproduced against today's code.

Harness timing is coarse: all 64 cells are exact multiples of 15.625 ms, the Windows XP clock() tick (checked arithmetically), each cell is one run (Iterates_Generations = 1), so the single-slot cpgf vs libsigc++ differences (781 vs 766, 719 vs 672, 468 vs 438 ms) are one to three ticks and not meaningful. The 46-47 ms 'native call' rows are about one cycle per iteration at 2 GHz, so the compiler collapsed those loops rather than timing a call. Boost.Signals2 ran with its default mutex (a thread-safe signal against two unsynchronized ones; a dummy_mutex signal was not tried), and the Boost single-slot rows invoke a signals2::slot directly.

Current GCallbackList::operator() forwards the same argument pack to every callback with std::forward inside the loop: for a by-value parameter such as void (std::string) called with an rvalue, the first slot moves the string out and later slots receive a moved-from value (read in the code; a self-written mimic of the same forwarding loop printed 'payload' then two empty strings). Its operator= overloads also lack return statements and call swap(std::move(other)) on a non-const lvalue-reference swap.

The inline buffer is sized as one pointer plus one member-function pointer (24 bytes on x86-64 GCC/Clang), but a member-function callback stores the table pointer, object pointer and member pointer (32 bytes in a self-written layout mimic), so every member-function callback is heap-allocated on construction and on every copy (add() copies). Removing or clearing a callback from inside its own invocation destroys it mid-call.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: SimpleSignal is the closer sibling (also beats Boost.Signals2 and libsigc++, measured against a single-thread Boost build) and the author's own eventpp supersedes cpgf's callback list, so prefer either for new code; pick cpgf only when you already depend on it. For a single type-erased callable, the std::function replacements (inplace_function, bdiamand Delegate, SmallFunction, woid) have current benchmarks against std::function, which cpgf lacks.
verified_claims_summary: doc/callback-benchmark.md (migrated in 2019 from cpgf.org, harness committed 2011) times 100M single-callback calls and 10M emissions of signals with 0 to 50 slots on a Pentium Dual E2180 under Windows XP with VC 9 -O2 and MinGW GCC 4.5.2 -O3: cpgf ties libsigc++ 2.2.8 on single calls and is 1.8x to 6.7x faster than invoking a Boost.Signals2 1.46 slot; on emission it is 4.3x faster than libsigc++ at 5 slots (VC 9, 641 vs 2734 ms), 1.17x at 50 slots, and 9.6x to 13.7x faster than the default mutex-protected Boost.Signals2 signal. Those numbers belong to the pre-2017 C++03 implementation.
status_note: Abandoned: the README says cpgf is not continued and sends callback users to eventpp and reflection users to metapp; last commit 2022-05-22, last change to the callback headers 2017-03-05; Apache-2.0 and the two callback headers are small enough to vendor, but the current GCallbackList has the forwarding and assignment bugs noted above.
